summary: This informational report reviews the Triggered Extensions to RIP in RFC 2091 and the experience gained from implementing them. It was written to satisfy the IETF's requirement that routing protocols be documented against a standard set of criteria.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card that checks how well a new homework method worked after students actually tried it.

questions: why triggered rip better than demand rip
subtitle: Protocol analysis of RIP extensions for efficient routing on demand circuits.

tldr.problem: Standard RIP periodically sends routing updates across all links, which is wasteful on expensive Wide Area Networks with dial-up or switched connections.
tldr.mechanism: Triggered RIP sends routing updates only when the routing database changes, and relies on the underlying connection manager to establish circuits only when needed, reducing unnecessary traffic.
tldr.outcome: Triggered RIP proved more efficient than the earlier Demand RIP approach and became the preferred method for routing on cost-sensitive WAN links.

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: Updates only on changes, not periodic broadcasts

today: RFC 2092 is Informational and not obsoleted. While Triggered RIP itself has been superseded by modern routing protocols, its core principle of event-driven updates rather than periodic broadcasts remains influential in routing protocol design.

sections.title: Analyzing Triggered RIP
sections.content:
This RFC analyzes the Triggered Extensions to RIP to Support Demand Circuits, specified in RFC 2091. It documents key features of this protocol and reports implementation experience from vendors. Triggered RIP extends the Routing Internet Protocol (RIP) and RIP-2 to run cost-effectively on Wide Area Networks like X.25, ISDN, Frame Relay, and dial-up links, where frequent periodic updates would be prohibitively expensive.

The RFC is part of the IETF's effort to evaluate routing protocols against standard criteria. As a result of Triggered RIP's advantages, an earlier alternative called Demand RIP was proposed for obsolescence.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a report card that explains how a new version of a routing protocol works better when computers don't have to talk constantly.

sections.title: Core Design of Triggered RIP
sections.content:
Triggered RIP keeps the same basic algorithms and packet formats as standard RIP when running on Local Area Networks, allowing transparent interoperability. On WANs, it operates differently: instead of periodic broadcasts, routing information is sent only when the database changes. Each update is retransmitted until acknowledged, and information received is not timed out automatically.

A circuit manager running below the IP layer establishes circuits on demand only when there is data to transfer. After a period of inactivity, the circuit is closed. If connection fails, the circuit manager signals the routing application, which then tries again at increasing intervals. When successful, it signals the routing application that the circuit is up.
sections.plainLanguage: The smart part is that the router only calls when it has something to say, and hangs up when done, saving money on expensive long-distance calls.

sections.title: Triggered Updates and Requirements
sections.content:
Updates are sent only when an event changes the routing database. The RIP response packet format is modified with a different command field to include sequence numbers, and a separate acknowledgement packet is defined. This contrasts with periodic flooding of the entire database.

Triggered RIP requires an underlying mechanism to detect unreachability in a finite, predictable period. For technologies using PPP, either Echo Request/Response or Link Quality Monitoring must detect black holes—cases where routing information gets stuck or returns fail to respond. Technologies without PPP must have an equivalent 'are-you-there' mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Updates only go out when routing info actually changes, and the system keeps checking if the link is alive so bad information doesn't get stuck forever.

sections.title: Real-World Implementation
sections.content:
At the time of writing, two completed implementations were known. The Xyplex implementation supports IP RIP-1, IP RIP-2, IPX RIP, and IPX SAP with testing on X.25, ISDN, Frame Relay, V42bis CSU/DSUs, and asynchronous modems. The implementation has only one outstanding acknowledgement per peer partner and has been tested for interoperability with various router implementations on Ethernet LANs.

The DEC implementation supports IP RIP-1 over ISDN, Frame Relay, leased lines and V.25bis. The Xyplex and DEC implementations demonstrated interoperability over ISDN without problems, proving the approach works across vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different companies successfully built this system and tested it together, proving the idea really works in practice.

sections.title: Advantages Over Demand RIP
sections.content:
Triggered RIP has significant efficiency advantages over Demand RIP. When routing information changes, Demand RIP sends the full routing database to its partner, while Triggered RIP sends only the changed information, dramatically decreasing data volume during route changes. Triggered RIP receivers apply changes immediately upon receiving each packet, reducing memory requirements compared to Demand RIP's approach of storing the full update before applying changes.

Demand RIP also has a 255-fragment limit on updates, restricting the size of routing databases that can be propagated. Triggered RIP lifts this restriction. In all other respects they perform the same function.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending your whole address book when one person moves, Triggered RIP sends only the update, saving time and space.
